claim: Secretory and endolysosomal fusion events are driven by SNAREs and cofactors, including Sec17/α-SNAP, Sec18/NSF, and Sec1/Munc18 (SM) proteins.
source: Secretory and endolysosomal fusion events are driven by SNAREs and cofactors, including Sec17/α-SNAP, Sec18/NSF, and Sec1/Munc18 (SM) proteins.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the molecular machinery of membrane fusion.

claim: SM proteins are essential for fusion in vivo.
source: SMs are essential for fusion in vivo, but the basis of this requirement is enigmatic.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about SM protein function.

claim: SM proteins Sly1 and Vps33 directly shield SNARE complexes from Sec17- and Sec18-mediated disassembly.
source: We now report that, in addition to their established roles as fusion accelerators, SM proteins Sly1 and Vps33 directly shield SNARE complexes from Sec17- and Sec18-mediated disassembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro disassembly assays shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Wild-type Sly1 and Vps33 function are required to withstand overproduction of Sec17 in vivo.
source: In vivo, wild-type Sly1 and Vps33 function are required to withstand overproduction of Sec17.
evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2 demonstrating growth defects in SM mutants when Sec17 is overproduced.

claim: Sly1 and Vps33 impede SNARE complex disassembly by Sec18 and ATP in vitro.
source: In vitro, Sly1 and Vps33 impede SNARE complex disassembly by Sec18 and ATP.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro disassembly assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sec17 directly promotes selective loading of Sly1 and Vps33 onto cognate SNARE complexes.
source: Unexpectedly, Sec17 directly promotes selective loading of Sly1 and Vps33 onto cognate SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is supported by binding assays shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: A large thermodynamic barrier limits SM binding to SNARE complexes.
source: A large thermodynamic barrier limits SM binding, implying that significant conformational rearrangements are involved.
evidence: This is supported by temperature-dependence experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Sec17 and SMs accelerate fusion mediated by cognate SNARE complexes and protect them from NSF-mediated disassembly.
source: In a working model, Sec17 and SMs accelerate fusion mediated by cognate SNARE complexes and protect them from NSF-mediated disassembly, while mis-assembled or non-cognate SNARE complexes are eliminated through kinetic proofreading by Sec18.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Mis-assembled or non-cognate SNARE complexes are eliminated through kinetic proofreading by Sec18.
source: In a working model, Sec17 and SMs accelerate fusion mediated by cognate SNARE complexes and protect them from NSF-mediated disassembly, while mis-assembled or non-cognate SNARE complexes are eliminated through kinetic proofreading by Sec18.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: During docking, SNAREs on apposed vesicle and target membranes oligomerize in trans, 'zippering' into an ultrastable coiled-coil bundle.
source: During docking, SNAREs on apposed vesicle and target membranes oligomerize in trans, 'zippering' into an ultrastable coiled-coil bundle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE function, supported by citations (Hanson et al., 1997; Nichols et al., 1997; Sutton et al., 1998; Fasshauer et al., 2002).

claim: SNARE zippering pulls the membranes into tight apposition, locally deforming and dehydrating the bilayers to initiate fusion and compartmental mixing.
source: SNARE zippering pulls the membranes into tight apposition, locally deforming and dehydrating the bilayers to initiate fusion and compartmental mixing (Hanson et al., 1997; Nichols et al., 1997; Sutton et al., 1998; Fasshauer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE function, supported by citations.

claim: Following fusion, individual SNAREs are entrapped within stable, fusion-inactive cis-complexes.
source: Following fusion, individual SNAREs are entrapped within stable, fusion-inactive cis-complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE complex states after fusion.

claim: Sec17 binds the cis-SNARE complex and recruits Sec18 to separate the SNAREs.
source: To separate the SNAREs and energize them for additional instances of trans-complex assembly and membrane fusion, Sec17 binds the cis-SNARE complex, in turn recruiting Sec18.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE disassembly, supported by citations (Sollner et al., 1993; Mayer et al., 1996; Hanson et al., 1997; Littleton et al., 1998; Grote et al., 2000; Wimmer et al., 2001; Marz et al., 2003; Cipriano et al., 2013).

claim: Sec18, a hexameric AAA-family ATPase, disassembles the cis-SNARE complex and ejects Sec17.
source: Sec18, a hexameric AAA-family ATPase, disassembles the cis-SNARE complex and ejects Sec17 (Sollner et al., 1993; Mayer et al., 1996; Hanson et al., 1997; Littleton et al., 1998; Grote et al., 2000; Wimmer et al., 2001; Marz et al., 2003; Cipriano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Sec18 function, supported by citations.

claim: SNAREs alone can fuse membranes in vitro.
source: SNAREs alone can fuse membranes in vitro (Weber et al., 1998), but fusion in vivo requires additional cofactors including regulatory small G proteins, compartment-specific tethers, and proteins of the SM family (Jackson and Chapman, 2006; Wickner and Schekman, 2008; Südhof and Rothman, 2009; Yu and Hughson, 2010; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Fusion in vivo requires additional cofactors including regulatory small G proteins, compartment-specific tethers, and proteins of the SM family.
source: SNAREs alone can fuse membranes in vitro (Weber et al., 1998), but fusion in vivo requires additional cofactors including regulatory small G proteins, compartment-specific tethers, and proteins of the SM family (Jackson and Chapman, 2006; Wickner and Schekman, 2008; Südhof and Rothman, 2009; Yu and Hughson, 2010; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SM proteins are SNARE-interacting ∼600 residue proteins with a highly conserved tertiary fold.
source: SM proteins are SNARE-interacting ∼600 residue proteins with a highly conserved tertiary fold (Carr and Rizo, 2010; Rizo and Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SM protein structure, supported by citations.

claim: Four SM subfamilies are essential for fusion within specific subcellular domains: ER and Golgi (Sly1), plasma membrane (Sec1/Munc18), endosomes (Vps45), and late endolysosomal organelles (Vps33).
source: Four SM subfamilies are essential for fusion within specific subcellular domains: ER and Golgi (Sly1; Cao and Barlowe, 2000; Dascher et al., 1991); plasma membrane (Sec1/Munc18; Grote et al., 2000; Harrison et al., 1994; Hosono et al., 1992; Novick et al., 1981; Verhage et al., 2000; Weimer et al., 2003); endosomes (Vps45; Cowles et al., 1994; Piper et al., 1994); and late endolysosomal organelles (Vps33; Banta et al., 1990; Wada et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SM protein localization and function, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The in vivo SM requirement is so general and so stringent that SMs are now considered, along with SNAREs, to be components of the core fusion machinery.
source: The in vivo SM requirement is so general and so stringent that SMs are now considered, along with SNAREs, to be components of the core fusion machinery (Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement of current scientific consensus, supported by a citation.

claim: Different SMs have divergent SNARE binding modalities.
source: A major reason for the proliferation of models is that different SMs have divergent SNARE binding modalities (Carr and Rizo, 2010; Rizo and Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SM protein diversity, supported by citations.

claim: SMs share a core ability to bind cognate ternary or quaternary SNARE bundles.
source: However, accruing evidence suggests that SMs share a core ability to bind cognate ternary or quaternary SNARE bundles (Carr et al., 1999; Scott et al., 2004; Carpp et al., 2006; Togneri et al., 2006; Dulubova et al., 2007; Kramer and Ungermann, 2011; Lobingier and Merz, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Sec1 and Munc18-1 accelerate SNARE-mediated liposome fusion by several-fold.
source: Indeed, Sec1 and Munc18-1 accelerate SNARE-mediated liposome fusion by several-fold (Scott et al., 2004; Shen et al., 2007; Rathore et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Munc18-1 stimulates liposome fusion more efficiently in concert with the specialist exocytosis cofactors Munc13 and synaptotagmin.
source: This acceleration is contingent on initial reaction conditions, and recent experiments show that Munc18-1 stimulates liposome fusion more efficiently in concert with the specialist exocytosis cofactors Munc13 and synaptotagmin (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Vps33, Vps45, and Sly1 accelerate liposome fusion, but with nearly absolute requirements for additional factors including Rab proteins and tethering factors.
source: Similarly, Vps33, Vps45, and Sly1 accelerate liposome fusion, but with nearly absolute requirements for additional factors including Rab proteins and tethering factors (Hickey et al., 2009; Ohya et al., 2009; Furukawa and Mima, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sec18 and Sec17 can disassemble pre-fusion trans-SNARE complexes in vitro.
source: In vitro, Sec18 and Sec17 can disassemble pre-fusion trans-SNARE complexes and can prevent the fusion of intact yeast lysosomal vacuoles or liposomes (Ungermann et al., 1998; Rohde et al., 2003; Mima et al., 2008; Stroupe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Premature SNARE disassembly was impeded by the Vps-C tethering complex HOPS.
source: Premature SNARE disassembly was impeded by the Vps-C tethering complex HOPS (Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The protective activity of HOPS was hypothesized to reside within its SM subunit Vps33.
source: This protective activity of HOPS was hypothesized to reside within its SM subunit Vps33, which is necessary and sufficient for HOPS binding to the vacuole SNARE complex (Lobingier and Merz, 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous work, supported by a citation.

claim: Vps33 is necessary and sufficient for HOPS binding to the vacuole SNARE complex.
source: This protective activity of HOPS was hypothesized to reside within its SM subunit Vps33, which is necessary and sufficient for HOPS binding to the vacuole SNARE complex (Lobingier and Merz, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Munc18-1, acting in concert with Munc13 and synaptotagmin, facilitated SNARE-mediated liposome fusion in the presence of otherwise inhibitory concentrations of NSF and α-SNAP.
source: Similarly, Munc18-1, acting in concert with Munc13 and synaptotagmin, facilitated SNARE-mediated liposome fusion in the presence of otherwise inhibitory concentrations of NSF and α-SNAP (Sec18 and Sec17; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of NSF and α-SNAP, Munc18 and Munc13 had little or no effect on the extent of SNARE-mediated liposome fusion when compared to fusion driven solely by SNAREs and synaptotagmin.
source: In the absence of NSF and α-SNAP, Munc18 and Munc13 had little or no effect on the extent of SNARE-mediated liposome fusion when compared to fusion driven solely by SNAREs and synaptotagmin.
evidence: This is a statement about previous experimental findings.

claim: Direct protection of a SNARE complex by an SM has not been experimentally demonstrated prior to this study.
source: However, central predictions of these models are still untested. Direct protection of a SNARE complex by an SM has not been experimentally demonstrated, and it is unknown whether SM proteins functionally interact (or compete) with the disassembly machinery in living cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: Sec17 and Sec18 overproduction in wild-type VPS33 cells caused normal growth at either 30°C or 37°C.
source: When Sec17 and Sec18 were overproduced in wild-type VPS33 cells, growth was normal at either standard temperature (30°C) or at 37°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Sec17 and Sec18 overproduction in mutant vps33car cells caused severe growth defects at 37°C.
source: In marked contrast, Sec17 and Sec18 overproduction in mutant vps33car cells caused severe growth defects at 37°C (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There was little or no growth defect when Sec17 and Sec18 were overproduced in vps41Δ cells.
source: There was little or no growth defect when Sec17 and Sec18 were overproduced in vps41Δ cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Overproduction of Sec17, or Sec17 and Sec18 together, had almost no effect on growth of VPS33 cells, with or without added Zn2+.
source: Overproduction of Sec17, Sec18, or both together had almost no effect on growth of VPS33 cells, with or without added Zn2+ (Figure 1B, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: vps33car mutants grew almost as well as VPS33 cells, but when Sec17, or Sec17 and Sec18 were overproduced together, the vps33car mutants grew slowly.
source: vps33car mutants grew almost as well as VPS33 cells, but when Sec17, or Sec17 and Sec18 were overproduced together, the vps33car mutants grew slowly (Figure 1B, middle panel), a defect markedly enhanced by 1 mM Zn2+ (Figure 1B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sec17 overproduction in vps33car cells, but not in wild-type cells, significantly impaired Sna3-fLuc sorting.
source: Sec17 overproduction in vps33car cells, but not in wild-type cells, significantly impaired Sna3-fLuc sorting (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C using the LUCID assay.

claim: Full Vps33 function is required to withstand either Sec17 or Sec17 and Sec18 overproduction.
source: Together, the data show that full Vps33 function is required to withstand either Sec17 or Sec17 and Sec18 overproduction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Wild-type SLY1 cells grew normally when Sec17 and Sec18 were overproduced, alone or together.
source: Wild-type SLY1 cells grew normally when Sec17 and Sec18 were overproduced, alone or together (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overproduction of Sec17, or Sec17 and Sec18 together, profoundly impaired the growth of sly1ts mutants, even at permissive temperatures (24–26°C).
source: In contrast, overproduction of Sec17, or Sec17 and Sec18 together, profoundly impaired the growth of sly1ts mutants, even at permissive temperatures (24–26°C; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: sly1ts sec18-1 double mutants were inviable.
source: In independent work, sly1ts sec18-1 double mutants were inviable (Kosodo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Full, wild-type Sly1 and Vps33 function is required to buffer cells against perturbations of the SNARE disassembly machinery.
source: We conclude that full, wild-type Sly1 and Vps33 function is required to buffer cells against perturbations of the SNARE disassembly machinery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In the absence of SMs, Sec18 rapidly and completely disassembled the SNARE complexes.
source: In the absence of SMs, Sec18 rapidly and completely disassembled the SNARE complexes (Figure 3B,C, lanes 1–5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: SNARE disassembly by Sec18 required ATP and was blocked when Mg2+ was sequestered by EDTA.
source: Disassembly required ATP and was blocked when Mg2+ was sequestered by EDTA (Figure 3B,C, compare lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Pre-incubation with SMs (Sly1 or Vps33) delayed, but did not prevent, SNARE disassembly.
source: Pre-incubation with SMs (Sly1 or Vps33) delayed, but did not prevent, SNARE disassembly (Figure 3B,C, lanes 7–11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Pre-incubation with Sly1 decreased the rate of SNARE disassembly by 63 ± 9%.
source: The effect of Sly1 was quantified: pre-incubation with the Sly1 decreased the rate of disassembly by 63 ± 9% (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sly1 protected Golgi SNARE complexes assembled on Sed5 full cytoplasmic domain as well as on Sed5 SNARE domain.
source: However, Sly1 also protected Golgi SNARE complexes assembled on Sed5 full cytoplasmic domain rather than Sed5 SNARE domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The ability of the Sly1 and Vps33 preparations to impede SNARE disassembly was heat labile.
source: In control reactions the ability of the Sly1 and Vps33 preparations to impede SNARE disassembly was heat labile (Figure 3D,E, compare lanes 3 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Omitting the pre-incubation step reduced both SM binding and SNARE complex protection.
source: Omitting the pre-incubation step reduced both SM binding and SNARE complex protection (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: At the low concentrations of free SNAREs liberated by disassembly, no re-assembly of SNARE complexes was detected within 30 min in either the absence or presence of SM.
source: At the low concentrations of free SNAREs liberated by disassembly, no re-assembly of SNARE complexes was detected within 30 min in either the absence or presence of SM (Figure 4B,C, compare lanes 1 and 3, and lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: After complete disassembly, re-assembly occurred when additional Qb, Qc, and R-SNAREs were added, but the rates of re-assembly were not increased by either Vps33 or Sly1.
source: After complete disassembly, additional Qb, Qc, and R-SNAREs were added along with the EDTA quench (Figure 4B,C, compare lanes 5 and 6). Under these conditions re-assembly occurred, but the rates of re-assembly were not increased by either Vps33 or Sly1, in accord with previous reports that these SMs do not accelerate SNARE assembly in solution (Kosodo et al., 2002; Peng and Gallwitz, 2002; Hickey and Wickner, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C, and citations to previous literature.

claim: Vps33 and Sly1 kinetically impair, but do not prevent, Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly.
source: We conclude that Vps33 and Sly1 kinetically impair, but do not prevent, Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Vps33 likely accounts for the ability of HOPS to shield trans-SNARE complexes from premature disassembly.
source: Because Vps33 is both necessary and sufficient for HOPS binding to SNARE core bundles (Lobingier and Merz, 2012), Vps33 likely accounts for the ability of HOPS to shield trans-SNARE complexes from premature disassembly (Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Protection of trans-SNARE complexes from Sec18/NSF may be a more general feature of SM biochemistry.
source: Because Vps33 and Sly1 exhibit similar activities, protection of trans-SNARE complexes from Sec18/NSF may be a more general feature of SM biochemistry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings with two different SM proteins.

claim: Up to three copies of Sec17/α-SNAP bind per SNARE complex bundle.
source: Up to three copies of Sec17/α-SNAP bind per SNARE complex bundle (Hanson et al., 1997; Fleming et al., 1998; Marz et al., 2003; Vivona et al., 2013), and α-SNAP can competitively displace the presynaptic Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin from neuronal SNARE complexes (Sollner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: α-SNAP can competitively displace the presynaptic Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin from neuronal SNARE complexes.
source: Up to three copies of Sec17/α-SNAP bind per SNARE complex bundle (Hanson et al., 1997; Fleming et al., 1998; Marz et al., 2003; Vivona et al., 2013), and α-SNAP can competitively displace the presynaptic Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin from neuronal SNARE complexes (Sollner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Vps33 binds the vacuole SNARE complex with low µM affinity.
source: As we previously reported (Lobingier and Merz, 2012), Vps33 binds the vacuole SNARE complex with low µM affinity (Figure 5A, lane 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to previous work.

claim: Sec17 addition strongly stimulated Vps33 binding to the SNARE complex.
source: But rather than competing, Sec17 addition strongly stimulated Vps33 binding to the SNARE complex (Figure 5A, lane 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The stoichiometry of Sec17 binding was unaltered when Vps33 was also bound.
source: Importantly, the stoichiometry of Sec17 binding was unaltered when Vps33 was also bound (Figure 5A, compare lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sec17 stimulation of Vps33 binding to the SNARE complex depended on the Sec17 concentration and tracked with Sec17 occupancy on the complex.
source: Sec17 stimulation of Vps33 binding to the SNARE complex depended on the Sec17 concentration and tracked with Sec17 occupancy on the complex (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sec17 increased the apparent affinity of Vps33 for SNARE complex by more than 5-fold (from KD(obs) = 1.60 ± 0.10 μM to 0.30 ± 0.01 μM).
source: Vps33-SNARE complex binding was saturable (Figure 5C), and Sec17 increased the apparent affinity of Vps33 for SNARE complex by more than 5-fold (from KD(obs) = 1.60 ± 0.10 μM to 0.30 ± 0.01 μM).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Under saturation binding conditions, Sec17–Vps33–SNARE complexes assembled in apparent 1:3:1 stoichiometry.
source: Under saturation binding conditions, Sec17–Vps33–SNARE complexes assembled in apparent 1:3:1 stoichiometry (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Vps33 bound to SNARE complex equally well in the presence of free-plus-bound Sec17 or to SNARE–Sec17 complex from which excess unbound Sec17 had been removed.
source: Vps33 bound to SNARE complex equally well in the presence of free-plus-bound Sec17 (Figure 5E, lane 2) or to SNARE–Sec17 complex from which excess unbound Sec17 had been removed (Figure 5E, lane 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Vps33 binding is stimulated by Sec17 on the SNARE complex, not by Sec17 in solution.
source: Thus, Vps33 binding is stimulated by Sec17 on the SNARE complex, not by Sec17 in solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5E.

claim: Addition of bovine serum albumin (BSA) in place of Sec17 had no effect on Vps33 binding to SNARE complex.
source: In a further control, addition of bovine serum albumin (BSA) in place of Sec17 had no effect on Vps33 binding to SNARE complex (Figure 5E, lane 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SNARE complex and Sec17 bound efficiently to immobilized Vps33 only when both were present.
source: SNARE complex and Sec17 bound efficiently to immobilized Vps33 only when both were present (Figure 5E, compare lane 4 to lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SNARE complexes and Sec17 bind Vps33 through a cooperative mechanism involving all three components.
source: SNARE complexes and Sec17 therefore bind Vps33 through a cooperative mechanism involving all three components.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5F.

claim: Sly1 was previously shown to avidly bind the terminal N-peptide of the Qa-SNARE Sed5.
source: Sly1 was previously shown to avidly bind the terminal N-peptide of the Qa-SNARE Sed5.
evidence: This is a statement of previous findings.

claim: N-peptide binding is dispensable for Sly1 function in vivo.
source: However, N-peptide binding is dispensable for Sly1 function in vivo (Bracher and Weissenhorn, 2002; Peng and Gallwitz, 2002, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Little or no Sly1 bound to the Golgi SNARE bundle lacking the N-peptide and Habc domains.
source: As in previous work (Peng and Gallwitz, 2004) little or no Sly1 bound to the Golgi SNARE bundle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to previous work.

claim: In the presence of Sec17, Sly1 binding to the Golgi SNARE bundle was dramatically stimulated.
source: In the presence of Sec17, however, Sly1 binding was dramatically stimulated (Figure 6A, compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Sly1 binding to SNARE complex depended on the Sec17 concentration and tracked with Sec17 occupancy on the complex.
source: As with Vps33, Sly1 binding to SNARE complex depended on the Sec17 concentration and tracked with Sec17 occupancy on the complex (Figure 6B, lanes 1-6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Sec17 did not associate with, or impede formation of, binary complexes between Sly1 and the N-peptide of full-length Sed5.
source: Sec17 did not associate with, or impede formation of, binary complexes between Sly1 and the N-peptide of full-length Sed5 (Figure 6B, lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Sec17 stimulates Sly1–SNARE complex association, but Sec17 does not efficiently bind Sly1 or Sed5 in the absence of an assembled SNARE complex.
source: Thus, Sec17 stimulates Sly1–SNARE complex association, but Sec17 does not efficiently bind Sly1 or Sed5 in the absence of an assembled SNARE complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6B.

claim: Sly1 bound to the Sec17–SNARE complex saturably and with moderate affinity (KD(obs) = 1.0 ± 0.1 µM).
source: Sly1 bound to the Sec17–SNARE complex saturably and with moderate affinity (Figure 6C; KD(obs) = 1.0 ± 0.1 µM).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the absence of Sec17, little or no Sly1 bound the SNARE bundle at concentrations up to 15 µM.
source: In the absence of Sec17, little or no Sly1 bound the SNARE bundle at concentrations up to 15 µM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Under saturation conditions the SNARE complex, Sec17, and Sly1 assembled in apparent 1:3:1 stoichiometry.
source: Under saturation conditions the SNARE complex, Sec17, and Sly1 assembled in apparent 1:3:1 stoichiometry, consistent with the results for Vps33 (Figures 5D and 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Sly1 binding was promoted by SNARE-bound Sec17 rather than Sec17 in solution.
source: As with Vps33, Sly1 binding was promoted by SNARE-bound Sec17 rather than Sec17 in solution (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The Sec17 concentration required to saturate Golgi SNARE complex was about four-fold greater than for vacuole SNARE complex.
source: The Sec17 concentration required to saturate Golgi SNARE complex was about four-fold greater than for vacuole SNARE complex (compare the Sec17 curves in Figures 5B and 6B).
evidence: This is an observation based on comparison of experimental data in Figures 5B and 6B.

claim: No increase in Sly1 binding to Golgi SNARE complexes was observed when BSA was added instead of Sec17.
source: No increase in Sly1 binding to Golgi SNARE complexes was observed when BSA was added instead of Sec17 (Figure 6E, lane 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Sly1, like Vps33, binds SNARE–Sec17 complexes through a cooperative mechanism.
source: Sly1, like Vps33, binds SNARE–Sec17 complexes through a cooperative mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6F.

claim: SNARE complex was retained by GST-Sly1 only in the presence of Sec17.
source: GST-tagged Sly1 was immobilized and assayed for binding of soluble SNARE complex, Sec17, or both (Figure 6F). SNARE complex was retained by GST-Sly1 only in the presence of Sec17, and Sec17 was retained most efficiently on GST-Sly1 when SNARE complexes were present.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Sec17 was retained most efficiently on GST-Sly1 when SNARE complexes were present.
source: GST-tagged Sly1 was immobilized and assayed for binding of soluble SNARE complex, Sec17, or both (Figure 6F). SNARE complex was retained by GST-Sly1 only in the presence of Sec17, and Sec17 was retained most efficiently on GST-Sly1 when SNARE complexes were present.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Sec17 did not detectably interact with Sly1 when Sly1 was tethered to the GST-Sed5 N-peptide.
source: However, Sec17 did not detectably interact with Sly1 when Sly1 was tethered to the GST-Sed5 N-peptide (Figure 6B, lanes 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Sec17 promotes Sly1 and Vps33 loading onto SNARE complexes through a cooperative mechanism.
source: We conclude that Sec17 promotes Sly1 and Vps33 loading onto SNARE complexes through a cooperative mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The resulting assemblies contain three Sec17 molecules and one SM per quaternary SNARE bundle.
source: The resulting assemblies contain three Sec17 molecules and one SM per quaternary SNARE bundle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stoichiometry data in Figures 5D and 6D.

claim: Sec17 and its mammalian homolog α-SNAP are capable of engaging all SNARE complexes.
source: Sec17 and its mammalian homolog α-SNAP are capable of engaging all SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Sec17/α-SNAP function.

source: There was little Sly1 dissociation at 4°C and slightly more at 30°C (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), indicating that elevated temperature promotes productive SM–SNARE association rather than stabilizing extant SM–SNARE complexes.

source: These observations indicate that the temperature dependence of SM binding is due to rate-limiting steps in SM–SNARE association rather than dissociation.

source: A possible interpretation is that Vps33 and Sly1 slowly interconvert between ground states unable to bind SNARE complexes and activated, binding-competent, states.

source: SNARE-bound Sec17—and perhaps other docking factors—would then elicit or stabilize activated SM conformations to accelerate SM loading onto cognate SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Pre-incubation of Sly1 at 30°C did not accelerate subsequent Sly1 binding to Sec17-SNARE complexes.
source: Because pre-incubation of Sly1 at 30°C did not accelerate subsequent Sly1 binding to Sec17-SNARE complexes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), we suggest that elevated temperature increases the frequency of interconversion between the putative ground and binding-active conformations, rather than by stabilizing an activated conformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elevated temperature increases the frequency of interconversion between the putative ground and binding-active conformations, rather than by stabilizing an activated conformation.
source: Because pre-incubation of Sly1 at 30°C did not accelerate subsequent Sly1 binding to Sec17-SNARE complexes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2), we suggest that elevated temperature increases the frequency of interconversion between the putative ground and binding-active conformations, rather than by stabilizing an activated conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sec17 is a multifunctional SNARE complex adapter, capable of recruiting not only the disassembly ATPase Sec18 but also compartment-specific SMs that oppose Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly.
source: Sec17 is therefore a multifunctional SNARE complex adapter, capable of recruiting not only the disassembly ATPase Sec18 but also compartment-specific SMs that oppose Sec18-mediated SNARE disassembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: When an SM recognizes and binds a Sec17–SNARE complex, it promotes fusion in at least three ways: by directly impeding SNARE disassembly by Sec18, by augmenting the SNARE complex's fusogenic activity, and by accelerating fusion to shorten the pre-fusion complex's temporal exposure to disassembly by Sec18.
source: When an SM recognizes and binds a Sec17–SNARE complex (reaction iv), it promotes fusion in at least three ways. First, the bound SM directly impedes SNARE disassembly by Sec18. Second, the SM augments the SNARE complex's fusogenic activity. Third, by accelerating fusion, the SM shortens the pre-fusion complex's lifetime, thereby shortening its temporal exposure to disassembly by Sec18 (kinetic partitioning; Hardy and Randall, 1991).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: SMs function as true enzymes: they bind and stabilize on-pathway intermediates, protect these intermediates from side reactions, and accelerate the conversion of intermediates to end products.
source: In this view of fusion, SMs function as true enzymes: they bind and stabilize on-pathway intermediates, protect these intermediates from side reactions, and accelerate the conversion of intermediates to end products.
evidence: This is a conceptual model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: This model predicts the annihilation of pathway-specific fusion when SMs are deleted from living cells.
source: Crucially, this model predicts the annihilation of pathway-specific fusion when SMs are deleted from living cells—a result that holds across many different organisms and fusion pathways.
evidence: This is a prediction of the proposed model, supported by established knowledge.

claim: When SM function is compromised, pre-fusion SNARE complexes should be less fusogenic, persist for longer times, and be more exposed to premature disassembly by Sec17 and Sec18.
source: When SM function is compromised, pre-fusion SNARE complexes should be less fusogenic, persist for longer times, and be more exposed to premature disassembly by Sec17 and Sec18 (Figure 9B, reaction v).
evidence: This is a prediction of the proposed model.

claim: SNAREs, Sec17, SMs, and Sec18 have precisely the features required to implement a kinetic proofreading system.
source: A further implication of our working model is that SNAREs, Sec17, SMs, and Sec18 have precisely the features required to implement a kinetic proofreading system (Hopfield, 1974).
evidence: This is a conceptual implication of the proposed model, supported by a citation to the kinetic proofreading concept.

claim: For SNARE-mediated fusion in vivo, there would be a minimum of two discrimination events: nucleation of the trans-SNARE complex and positive selection of on-pathway SNARE bundles by SM proteins.
source: For SNARE-mediated fusion in vivo, there would be a minimum of two discrimination events. First, the nucleation of the trans-SNARE complex (an intermediate analogous to a Michaelis complex) has significant but not absolute intrinsic selectivity, derived mainly from packing interactions at the core of the SNARE bundle. Second, on-pathway SNARE bundles are positively selected by SM proteins.
evidence: This is a conceptual model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Sec17 detects the general shape and charge distribution of assembled SNARE bundles.
source: Sec17 detects the general shape and charge distribution of assembled SNARE bundles (Marz et al., 2003), while SMs identify pathway-specific SNARE configurations, protecting them from Sec18 and augmenting their forward fusogenic activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: SMs identify pathway-specific SNARE configurations, protecting them from Sec18 and augmenting their forward fusogenic activity.
source: Sec17 detects the general shape and charge distribution of assembled SNARE bundles (Marz et al., 2003), while SMs identify pathway-specific SNARE configurations, protecting them from Sec18 and augmenting their forward fusogenic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Error products—off-pathway, incorrectly assembled, or damaged SNARE complexes—would not be efficiently bound by SMs and would be fully exposed to Sec17 and Sec18-mediated disassembly.
source: Error products—off-pathway, incorrectly assembled, or damaged SNARE complexes—would not be efficiently bound by SMs (Figure 9B, reaction v). These complexes would fuse more slowly or not at all, and would be fully exposed to Sec17 and Sec18-mediated disassembly.
evidence: This is a prediction of the proposed kinetic proofreading model.

claim: Individual SNAREs readily enter into non-cognate, off-pathway, antiparallel or mis-registered complexes with substantial thermal stability and commensurately low off-rates.
source: Although SNAREs selectively drive fusion when complexed with cognate partners (McNew et al., 2000), individual SNAREs readily enter into non-cognate, off-pathway, antiparallel or mis-registered complexes with substantial thermal stability and commensurately low off-rates (Brunger et al., 2009; Furukawa and Mima, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Certain R-SNAREs (Nyv1, Snc2, Sec22) drive fusion with non-cognate Q-SNAREs.
source: Moreover, certain R-SNAREs (Nyv1, Snc2, Sec22) drive fusion with non-cognate Q-SNAREs (McNew et al., 2000; Izawa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Compartment-specific tethers confer additional selectivity by accelerating the forward rate of cognate SNARE pairing, but this may not be sufficient.
source: Compartment-specific tethers confer additional selectivity by accelerating the forward rate of cognate SNARE pairing, but this may not be sufficient.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of tethering factors in ensuring SNARE specificity.

claim: 98% of late endosomes and lysosomes are adjacent to ER, generally within 30 nm or less.
source: For example, mammalian endosomes progressively associate with endoplasmic reticulum (ER) until 98% of late endosomes and lysosomes are adjacent to ER, generally within 30 nm or less (Friedman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Proofreading would emplace a last line of defense against SNARE assembly errors and consequent defects in cell architecture and function.
source: Proofreading would emplace a last line of defense against SNARE assembly errors and consequent defects in cell architecture and function.
evidence: This is a conceptual implication of the proposed kinetic proofreading model.

claim: At neuronal synapses, α-SNAP (Sec17) and the Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin compete for SNARE complex binding.
source: At neuronal synapses, α-SNAP (Sec17) and the Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin compete for SNARE complex binding (Sollner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Synaptotagmin may interact with the SM (Munc18-1) to protect pre-fusion complexes in a manner analogous to Sec17 and Vps33 or Sly1.
source: Within this specialized context (Fasshauer et al., 1998; Jackson and Chapman, 2008; Südhof and Rothman, 2009), synaptotagmin may interact with the SM (Munc18-1) to protect pre-fusion complexes in a manner analogous to Sec17 and Vps33 or Sly1.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to the neuronal system.

claim: Off-pathway cis-SNARE complexes undergo futile cycles of assembly and Sec18/NSF-mediated disassembly.
source: Off-pathway cis-SNARE complexes (e.g., Qa2-Qb-Qc; Fasshauer and Margittai, 2004; Fasshauer et al., 1997; Margittai et al., 2001; Pobbati et al., 2006), undergo futile cycles of assembly and Sec18/NSF-mediated disassembly, and it has been suggested that SMs might positively select activated pre-docking intermediates (Carr et al., 1999; Carr and Rizo, 2010; Kramer and Ungermann, 2011; Ma et al., 2013; Furukawa and Mima, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: High levels of Vps33 and Sly1 remain associated with Qa-SNARE domains following complex disassembly by Sec17 and Sec18.
source: In this context it is notable that high levels of Vps33 and Sly1 remain associated with Qa-SNARE domains following complex disassembly by Sec17 and Sec18 (Figure 3), raising the possibility that SNARE disassembly is coupled to the formation of SM-SNARE subcomplexes prior to docking.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: SNARE disassembly may be coupled to the formation of SM-SNARE subcomplexes prior to docking.
source: In this context it is notable that high levels of Vps33 and Sly1 remain associated with Qa-SNARE domains following complex disassembly by Sec17 and Sec18 (Figure 3), raising the possibility that SNARE disassembly is coupled to the formation of SM-SNARE subcomplexes prior to docking.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data in Figure 3.

source: The geometry of SNARE juxtamembrane domains in cis or trans, and especially the geometries of the membrane surfaces before and after fusion, may control whether Sec17 and SMs synergize or compete for binding.
evidence: This is a speculative consideration about factors that may influence SM-Sec17 interactions.

source: Consistent with this idea, Sec17 competes with the HOPS complex for binding to post-fusion cis-SNARE complexes on the yeast vacuole, as shown in meticulous co-isolation experiments (Collins et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

source: This Sec17-dependent fusion requires Rab signaling and the HOPS effector complex—including the SM Vps33—but is totally independent of Sec18 and ATP (Schwartz and Merz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

source: Vps33 and Sly1 binding to core SNARE bundles, with or without Sec17, is slow and rate-limited by temperature (Figure 8), implying that significant conformational transitions are required for assembly of SM–SNARE complexes.

source: The requirement for physiological (warm) temperatures in our in vitro assays may explain in part why SM–Sec17–SNARE interactions were not previously detected.

source: The central cavities of SMs are proposed binding sites for SNARE helical bundles and vary in the sizes of their openings, implying conformational flexibility (Bracher and Weissenhorn, 2001; Bar-On et al., 2011; Baker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The observations provide new empirical support for models in which SM proteins and perhaps SNAREs must undergo substantial conformational transitions to productively associate.
source: Our observations provide new empirical support for models in which SM proteins and perhaps SNAREs must undergo substantial conformational transitions to productively associate.
